full_judgment:
This Rule obtained u/s. 115(old) of the Code of Civil Procedure arises out of an application u/s. 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-emption. The learned Munsif, 3rd Court, Narail allowed the Misc. Judicial Case No. 206 of 1974 by Judgment and order dated 30-12-76. On appeal the learned District Judge, Jessore by his judgment and order dated 24-11-77 in Misc: Appeal No. 26 of 1977 reversed the findings of the learned Munsif, allowed the appeal and dismissed the Misc Case. 

 9. The only case in which it has been held that the choice of some holdings for pre-emption out of several holdings sold will be a case of partial pre-emption is the case cited by Mr. Chowdhury, namely, Salimuddin Mondal Vs. Mohitosh Biswas, 14 DLR 796, a Single Bench decision. That was a case under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The reason that weighed with the learned Judge is that under section 14(2) of the Bengal General Clauses Act the words "holding", "portion" and "share", though used in the singular, should include the plural. So, when several "holdings' are sold by the same transaction, the co-sharer tenant must apply for pre-emption in respect of "portions" or "shares" of all the "holdings" sold. It was argued that if several holdings are sold by one deed of sale then in fact it was more than one kabala and therefore the pre-emptor may ask for pre-emption in respect of one such transaction. The learned Judge repelled this contention and held that a sale of several properties by one deed of sale should be construed as one single transaction. The pre-emptor does not have the liberty to make a choice of his own and to take an arbitrary selection of one property out of several properties although he is in a position to ask for pre-emption as a co-sharer tenant with respect to all of them. "If the intending pre-emptor does not like a stranger to be a co-sharer tenant with respect to one particular holding it is difficult to understand how he might like the same stranger in regard to another part of the property conveyed by the same instrument." 

 10. The effect of the above decision is that the right of pre-emption accrues not only holding-wise but also transaction-wise. If several holdings are sold by one deed of sale, the pre-emptor must pre-empt the entire transaction if he is a co-sharer in all the holdings. This is not the effect and purport of section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, as held by several cases cited before. The clear intention of the legislature was to confer a right of pre-emption holding-wise and not transaction wise. Section 13 of the General Clauses Act is inapplicable here, because in the context of section 2(13) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, defining the word "holding", read with section 96(1) of the said Act, the right of pre-emption has not been conferred with reference to the number of properties transferred by a particular deed. A distinct right has been conferred in respect of a distinct holding. Section 13 of the General Clauses Act is inapplicable because the subject or context is repugnant. 

 13. The pre-empted kabala is dated 4-10-73.The petitioner claims knowledge of the sale on 27.8.74 corresponding to 10th Bhadra, 1381 BS and he fixed the Misc. Case on 17-14-74. The petitioner has stated as PW 1 that he knew about the sale on 27-8-74 from one Mukhles Shariff who as PW 2 corroborated him. PW 2 Mokhlcs Shariff, however, claims that he came to know of the sale from one Mobarek Kazi who has not been examined. PWs admit that the pre-emptee opposite parties are in possession but the petitioner has not adduced any evidence as to how and when they came to possess their purchased lands. Hence it must be assumed that the pre-emptees came into actual possession from the date of their purchase. It is also admitted that the vendor left the country after selling the case lands. The opposite parties gave evidence that the petitioner himself partitioned the case land and that there was a Salish. The learned District Judge observed that the Trial Court did not properly assess the evidence of OPWs 2-6. 

 14. Mr. Halder's objection to the treatment of the learned District Judge on the question of limitation is that (1) he had failed to discuss the evidence of 4 PWs, including the petitioner, (2) it is not correct that the petitioner has failed to adduce any evidence as to how and when the OPs came to possess the case lands. PW 4 has stated that the OPs went into possession of the suit lands 2 Katrick ago, deposing on 4-12-76. (3) the learned District Judge finds fault with the learned Munsif for not assessing the evidence of OPWs 2-6 properly, but he himself has not assessed their evidence at all. The alternative story set up by the OPs that the petitioner had knowledge of the sale from the beginning, has not been proved by the OPs at all. 

 15. No exception can be taken to the finding of the learned District Judge that "since the case is filed more than a year after the sale the onus is heavily on the petitioner to prove that he had no knowledge beyond 4 months next before the filing of the case. "The learned District Judge holds that the statement of the petitioner as PW 1 to the effect that he came to know of the sale on 27-8-74 has been corroborated by PW 2. If so, then on the learned District Judge's own showing the petitioner has discharged his onus to prove that he came to know of the sale on 27-8-74. The learned District Judge does not come to a definite finding that the petitioner has not discharged his onus to prove the said statement, nor does he say that without examining Mubarok Kazi the petitioner statement does not stand sufficiently corroborated. 

 17. True, the PWs admit that the OPs are in possession of the case lands but the learned District Judge has failed to discuss the evidence on record and has failed to take note of the statements of PW 3 and PW 4 as to when and how the OPs went into possession of the case lands.
